q: A bug report's To Reproduce section exists primarily to:
options: Turn the bug into a falsifiable input/output contract a maintainer can run
Prove the reporter read the code before filing
Satisfy a minimum character count on GitHub
Document which version the reporter preferred
explanation: Reading the code is not required — often impossible for the reporter.
There is no character quota; structure is for triage, not length.
Version preference is irrelevant; the version actually run matters.

q: Which describes real commit 509fcac69 in this checkout's history?
options: fix(token_counter): fix panic with GitHub Copilot (#4632) — a +3/-1 change in one file
feat: add a new provider integration across 9 crates
chore: bump workspace version to 1.49.0
fix(desktop): resolve UI freeze after renaming session
explanation: Large multi-crate feature work was not this commit's shape.
The version bump to 1.49.0 is dd8de0196, not this fix.
The desktop freeze fix is ec96aa059, a different PR.

q: Mid-bisect, git reports the current commit DOES show the bug. You run:
options: git bisect bad
git bisect good
git bisect skip
git bisect reset
explanation: good marks commits where the repro passes — this one failed.
skip is only for commits you cannot test (build breaks, unrelated crash).
reset aborts the whole bisect session and returns you to your branch.

q: `git bisect run .\check.ps1` interprets the script's behavior how?
options: Exit 0 = good, non-zero = bad; bisect replays the script on every midpoint
Any printed output line containing PASS means good
Exit 0 = bad, 125 = good, 1 = skip — one higher than manual convention
The script must call `git bisect bad` itself or the run errors
explanation: bisect run keys on the exit code, not on stdout text.
The convention is: 0 good, 1-127 (except 125) bad, 125 skip.
The script only signals via exit code; it never drives git itself.

q: Your 6-commit scratch history has a regression at commit 4. With a working repro script, manual midpoint bisect needs about how many repro runs?
options: 2 to 3 (log2 of the history)
5 (one per remaining commit)
1 (always the midpoint)
6 (worst case: every commit tested)
explanation: Testing every commit is linear search — exactly what bisect avoids.
A single run finds the buggy commit only by luck, not by search.
Worst case with bisect on 6 commits is 3 runs, not 6.

q: Fix this workflow error: you bisected and git said commit X is first bad, but your colleague says X also happens to be a merge commit. Your next step is:
options: Treat X as a hypothesis — read its diff and confirm the regression actually enters there
Restart with `git bisect start --first-parent` and delete the log
Report the bug against the maintainer and stop
Ignore the colleague; bisect output is authoritative
explanation: --first-parent is useful, but starting over before reading the diff wastes the session.
Bisect gave you a candidate; abandoning it to others skips the confirmation work.
On merge histories the reported commit is a starting point, not a verdict.

q: In the real clone, `git log --oneline -8 -- crates/goose/src/token_counter.rs` is the right first command because:
options: It constrains history to the file you suspect, making a fix-commit scan fast
It verifies the file still compiles
It fetches a fresh copy of the file from the remote
It shows which GitHub user owns the file
explanation: git log never compiles anything.
git log is local read-only history; fetching is git fetch.
Ownership lives in .github/CODEOWNERS, unrelated to git log path filtering.
